thread.title: GRASSLEY MIX-UP FUELS AGE QUESTIONS AS IOWA VOTERS HEAD TO POLLS | Next News Network
thread.title_full: GRASSLEY MIX-UP FUELS AGE QUESTIONS AS IOWA VOTERS HEAD TO POLLS | Next News Network

author: Gary Franchi
title: GRASSLEY MIX-UP FUELS AGE QUESTIONS AS IOWA VOTERS HEAD TO POLLS | Next News Network
text:
Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley arrived for an interview and began speaking to a member of his own staff as though she were the correspondent, according to an account circulating on social media. Following what was described as an uncomfortable pause, the staffer corrected Grassley and pointed him toward the journalist, the account states.
The claim was posted by the account @BulwarkOnline and has since been picked up across a range of feeds. The Bulwark account describes the episode in a single sentence, without naming the outlet involved, the journalist, the staffer, or the date and location of the interview. The account presents no video, audio, or transcript to support the description.
What is not in dispute is the broader context in which the claim landed. Age has become a live political topic in Iowa this cycle, even though the state's major-party candidates for Senate and governor are considerably younger than its senior senator. The oldest of the statewide nominees, Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek, is 47. Grassley, by contrast, first won public office during the Eisenhower administration, a fact his own campaign has never hidden and which has drawn renewed attention as the midterms approach.
The senator himself has addressed the subject of his age in recent weeks, offering what has been characterized as a rare acknowledgment of it while encouraging Iowans to vote for Zach Lahn, the Republican nominee for governor. Grassley also stumped for Iowa Republican candidates on Wednesday morning, urging party members to amplify their voices on social media to encourage the state's dominant registered base to turn out in November. Speaking at the Westside Conservative Club, Grassley told Iowa Republicans to "get people cranked up" on social media for the midterms and to "get over" grievances against fellow Republicans, according to coverage of the event by Little Village.
The staffer mix-up claim, as carried by @BulwarkOnline, is being repeated by other accounts without additional sourcing. The Bulwark's own newsletter has been promoting member-only programming, including an October 18 livestream featuring Pete Buttigieg alongside Sam, JVL, Sarah, and Tim, broadcast live from Charlotte, with members able to tune in from home in real time and join a live chat or watch on demand. That promotional material runs alongside the item about Grassley in the same feed, though the two are separate.
Readers encountering the claim should note what it does and does not contain. It does not identify the interview's outlet, the journalist who was waiting, the staffer who corrected the senator, or the setting. It offers no time stamp beyond the post itself. It provides no recording. It asserts a sequence of events — senator speaks to staffer, pause, correction, redirection — without documenting any part of it.
The claim's circulation matters in a state where age has become part of the political conversation, but the reaction is not evidence that the underlying episode occurred. In Iowa, the conversation about age has been driven in part by Grassley's long tenure and in part by the contrast with a younger field of candidates. Turek, at 47, sits near the generational boundary between Generation X and Millennials. The other statewide nominees are similarly younger than the incumbent senator. That contrast is what makes an account like the one posted by @BulwarkOnline travel.
Grassley's Wednesday appearance in Iowa was itself aimed at turnout. He told the Westside Conservative Club that Republicans should use social media to energize the party's registered base and that they should set aside internal grievances to focus on November. Those remarks are documented in press coverage of the event. The staffer mix-up claim, by contrast, is not documented in that coverage or in any other reporting reviewed.
Next News Network could not independently verify the claim that Grassley mistook a staffer for a journalist.
What remains is an account, posted by a single handle, repeated by others, arriving in the middle of a midterm cycle in which the senator's age is already a topic of discussion. Grassley has acknowledged that topic himself in recent weeks while campaigning for Lahn and other Iowa Republicans. Whether the specific episode described by @BulwarkOnline took place, and under what circumstances, is not established by anything currently circulating.
Voters in Iowa will render their own judgment in November. Until then, the claim will continue to move through feeds that have already shown an appetite for stories about age and elected officials. The account that started it offers one sentence. The rest is repetition.
Our Take
The press has spent years telling voters that questions about Chuck Grassley's age are out of bounds, and now it is amplifying an anonymous, unsourced claim that a staffer had to correct him mid-interview because it fits a narrative they have been pushing for months. Notice the structure: one account posts a sentence with no outlet, no journalist, no staffer, no video, no audio, no transcript, and no date — and the story is treated as though it happened. If this were a claim about a Democrat, the same people would demand the tape before running a word of it. Iowans deserve better than whisper campaigns laundered through feeds. If someone has the recording, release it. If they do not, they should stop trading in it.
